sections.h:
MOVEMENT OF HOPE

ECCLESIAL JOURNEY

GUIDES FOR CATECHESIS AND BIBLICAL HISTORY, FOR GROUP LEADERS

INTRODUCTION

“Not that we are competent of ourselves to claim anything as coming from us; our competence is from God, who has made us ministers” (2 Cor 3:5). “Neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth” (1 Cor 3:7)

And this is our hope as we offer you this small guide, which is meant above all to help the leaders in that task of evangelization which was the desire and the longing of Jesus when he sent out the apostles: “Go into all the world and proclaim the Gospel to the whole creation” (Mk 16:15).

It is a desire that Mother Rosa welcomed and lived out generously:

“I wish I had a hundred arms… I wish I could run everywhere and cry out that everyone should come to love you.”

The invitation to go and bring to every creature the good news of God’s love for every person is also, for the Movement, a primary task. The Statute reminds us: “Keeping in their hearts, like Mother Rosa, the primacy of evangelization for the spread of the faith, the members of the Movement also seek to reach – wherever possible – poor parishes or areas lacking a Christian presence, in order to make Jesus Christ known. Since the charism is a gift of God to the Church, the members of the Movement are to feel the joy and the urgency of announcing this gift to others, so that they too may begin or deepen their journey of faith, rediscovering their own baptism and embracing the spirituality of the Movement. To this end they work for the establishment and specific formation of other groups” (Statute, p. 34, a and b)

It is true that unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labour in vain (cf. Ps 127); yet that word of Jesus, “go… proclaim,” must urge us to do everything possible so that people may come to know the Lord who has “overcome the world” and has brought us all… “life in abundance”!

A) Therefore, to respect and foster this journey of knowledge and growth in faith, we think it is not good for brothers and sisters who ask to enter the Movement to be placed in a group that has already walked a certain stretch of the road. Only as an exception, and because it is not possible at the moment to gather enough people to start a new group, may one or two be received into a group that is already “adult.” But they should be made to understand that it is in their own interest to live through all the moments and stages by which the Movement structures its journey from the very beginning.

B) It is always prudent not to propose the Movement’s journey to those who already belong to other movements, associations or prayer groups, or who already live an adult faith in the Church. It is better, rather, remembering Mother Rosa’s longing to make Jesus known, to keep in mind above all those who live in suffering and loneliness, far from the faith and in ignorance of the Gospel promised to the poor…

C) Naturally, the service of leader for the groups that will be born will be entrusted to brothers and sisters who have already made the journey. A minimum of experience and of knowledge of the spirituality will help them to be truly brothers and sisters, attentive to the integration and growth of newcomers.

FIRST MEETING

Those brothers and sisters who, in whatever way, have come to know of the Movement and wish to learn about the Christian way of life it proposes will be invited to a first meeting. The importance of answering God’s call will be stressed to them: God wants to reach the human heart in many different ways, and so theirs as well! Only he can penetrate and change it. When he takes possession of a creature, he makes it holy: “You shall be holy, for I the Lord your God am holy” (Lev 19:2; 1 Pet 1:15; Mic 6:8). Only he can do this. In his mercy… he accomplishes the impossible! To respond to his promptings is already salvation!

The Lord loves human beings infinitely, every human being…: “This is the will of God, your sanctification” (1 Thess 4:3). He wants to sanctify, that is, to share with his creatures his very own life! But he knows the frailty of each one profoundly, and he knows that on their own, human beings would never manage.

Moreover, a person needs to feel supported by a community that lives the same ideal. This is why the Holy Spirit raises up in the Church countless gifts or charisms: movements, associations, groups… so many paths of differing spiritualities, not because all of them must be followed, but to give each person the possibility of feeling “called” on the path that best answers his or her spiritual needs, precisely because each person needs to relate to God according to his or her own nature, his or her own way of being.

All the paths present in the Church, therefore, have one single purpose: to lead people to holiness! And all of them tend to glorify God, bringing out his manifold wisdom and richness…

The Movement of Hope is called to live the charism and the spirituality of Rosa Gattorno who, through the holy Mother of Mary, Anna, rooted in the spirituality of the “Poor of Yahweh,” follows Christ, the “poor one” par excellence, contemplating Mary, the perfect model of the humble and the poor of the Lord.

After this first meeting, a series of catecheses will follow:

Call to holiness: … which is for everyone! Because all human beings were created in the image and likeness of God!

Sin: human beings experience their weakness and break off the dialogue

God’s mercy: “Where are you?”… it is always God’s tenderness that restores the dialogue with the human person.

The compassion of Jesus: the full revelation of God’s mercy and tenderness.

The necessity of prayer: in order to be… strong and to keep communion with the Father.

In the prayer of the poor: the Psalms, the prayer given by God to humankind.

FIRST CATECHESIS

THE CALL TO HOLINESS

“God, infinitely perfect and blessed in himself, in a plan of sheer goodness freely created man to make him share in his own blessed life. For this reason, at every time and in every place, God draws close to man. He calls man to seek him, to know him, to love him with all his strength… God calls men to become, in the Holy Spirit, his adopted children and therefore heirs of his blessed life.”

(Catechism of the Catholic Church, no. 1).

The Lord comes to seek us in a thousand ways, he invites us, he draws us, with one single purpose: he wants to accomplish a great work in each one of us; he wants to accomplish the impossible: he wants to make us holy! Out of each one of us he wants to make a masterpiece of grace. This is his will: our sanctification (1 Thessalonians 4:3). That is why he exhorts us with all the firmness of a caring father: “You shall be holy, for I the Lord your God am holy!” (Leviticus 19:2).

When we speak of holiness, we think of an impossible undertaking, beyond our abilities, and so, as we admire, for example, Saint Francis, Saint Clare, Saint Augustine… Mother Rosa, we take them to be privileged persons, and we easily exclaim: “How fortunate they are!” We suppose these creatures were born already holy! But experience teaches us that no one is born a saint (original sin, after all, has stained us all!); one becomes a saint, by way of a slow and arduous journey. We often stop at the finished work and do not take into account the process that led to such a “masterpiece.” That “process,” in fact, unfolds amid joys and sufferings, surges of enthusiasm and uncertainties, surrenders and doubts. In this difficult growth we need to be supported and encouraged: “But now thus says the Lord, he who created you, O Jacob, he who formed you, O Israel: ‘Fear not, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by name, you are mine. When you pass through the waters I will be with you; and through the rivers, they shall not overwhelm you; for I am the Lord your God, the Holy One of Israel, your Savior… Because you are precious in my eyes, and honored, and I love you… Fear not, for I am with you’” (Isaiah 43:1-5).

Those saints whom we admire believed this “word,” and today the Lord, through the mouth of the prophet, repeats it to us as well. All of us can set out on such a journey. It is the road walked by the Patriarchs, by the prophets, by the little “remnant,” by Jesus. All of them experienced their own weakness. Human nature, in the face of suffering, has always… balked! Even Jesus experienced that humiliation: in the temptations in the desert, in the anguish of Gethsemane, in the agony of the cross. But knowing the Father’s love made him triumph: “Begone, Satan! Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came and ministered to him” (Matthew 4:10-11).

“Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me; nevertheless not my will, but yours, be done.” And there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him” (Luke 22:42-43).

What matters is that this journey be made together with brothers and sisters:

God revealed himself to a people because he himself is “communion”; he made himself known as… TRINITY!

Let us make this invitation our own: “Now therefore, if you will obey my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my own possession among all peoples; for all the earth is mine, and you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exodus 19:5-6).

Human beings can therefore enjoy a full happiness, because God wished to offer his divine life, calling his creature to share in it. And “salvation” for man is precisely to welcome the God who gives himself!

From the beginning, God’s “word” opened a history, which began with creation: “God said: Let us make man in our image, after our likeness” (Genesis 1:26); and that history continues with every man who comes into this world… because that word which comes forth from the depths of the divine life wants to communicate itself, to be “heard,” “welcomed”… because that word… LOVES! (Cf. John 1:1-5, 14, 18; 3:16).

Man lives; he was created to be God’s “partner.” His being a person is for the sake of relating to the personal God, who calls him to account!

But this vocation… makes us tremble!

The creature is not God; God is wholly other…

A God who calls provokes bewilderment and mixed feelings of dread and fascination, which make man aware of his smallness, but also of his need for this strong and compelling presence that leads to life: “If you will obey my voice…” And this voice has resounded: “Give ear, O heavens, and I will speak…” (Deuteronomy 32:1-3).

And man learned to walk with God: “O Israel, if you would but listen to me!” (Psalm 81:9).

The prophet Isaiah feels lost before the God… “thrice holy,” a king of infinite majesty, the creator whose glory fills the whole earth, whom man cannot see and live (Cf. Exodus 33:18-23). But this prophet will have an experience of communion with God’s holiness! “Woe is me… for my eyes have seen!” (Isaiah 6:1-7). That voice inviting us to listen is therefore meant to propose a “covenant”: “Today, if you hear his voice, harden not your hearts” (Psalm 95:8).

Either man grasps this holiness, learns to know where prudence, strength and understanding are to be found, or he is truly lost (Cf. Baruch 3:9-14)! Either he trusts in this… holy ally, or man is defeated by the mystery of evil, of suffering, of death. Without God’s holiness, revealed to the world and entered into our history, we would end in nothingness (Cf. Psalm 28:1).

“My heart recoils within me, my compassion grows warm and tender… for I am God and not man, the Holy One in your midst!” (Hosea 11:7-9).

It is he, the holy God, who is the protagonist of history: he gives it life, becomes its support, its strength (Cf. Isaiah 10:20; 17:7-10; 41:14-20). He does not tire of speaking to barren, enslaved, despairing people: “Hear the word of the Lord, O nations, and declare it” (Jeremiah 31:10).

The Apostles too, heralds of this good news – of the holy God who became one of us to bring forgiveness and to free us from death – will call people to listen: “Men of Israel, hear these words…” (Acts 2:22).

“Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God is one Lord; and you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart…” (Deuteronomy 6:4-5).

That promise has been fulfilled: we can love God, because “in these last days he has spoken to us by a Son…” (Hebrews 1:2). Jesus will cry out this holiness, inviting us to share in it: “If anyone thirst, let him come…” (John 7:37-39), “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and would that it were already kindled!” (Luke 12:49); “I did not come to judge the world but to save the world… the Father who sent me has himself given me commandment what to say and what to speak. And I know that his commandment is eternal life!” (John 12:47-50).

God’s holiness fills our life with good things and directs it toward the fullness of happiness… It is true: man is poor and unhappy (Psalms 69:30 and 88:16): what is his experience of joy? Of stability? Of well-being? Of peace? Of security? Like Isaiah, one would want to cry out before the dazzling splendor of this divine life, “Woe is me, for I am lost!” Or, with Peter, in the presence of an abundant and unexpected catch of fish, to groan: “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man!” (Luke 5:8).

But that “word”… would always come pressing, inviting: “Fear not!” You may go on marveling: “What is man that you are mindful of him?” (Psalm 8). But you must praise God, because by that “word” you are called still to discover yourself a… “wonder” (Psalm 139)!

Jesus’ invitation to be perfect as the Father is perfect, then, is not absurd (Matthew 5:48 and Luke 6:35)!

Man can know God, can come to possess him (Cf. John 17:3)! “We shall be like him…” (1 John 3:1-2), “I write this to you… that you may know that you have eternal life…” (1 John 5:13).

Paul too, later on, will confirm to the Christian communities: “Christ Jesus… became for us… sanctification” (1 Corinthians 1:30), revealing that this is God’s… tireless will: “your sanctification!” (1 Thessalonians 4:3).

Experiencing the full breadth and depth of this divine holiness, which is the love with which God envelops man (Cf. Ephesians 3:17-19), the apostle will break into praise for this holy God, the “Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places, even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him in love, he destined us in love to be his sons through Jesus Christ” (Ephesians 1:1-14).

May the Lord “give you a spirit of wisdom and of revelation in the knowledge of him, having the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope to which he has called you…” (Ephesians 1:17-19).

(SEE APPENDIX NO. 1: “Christifideles laici,” nos. 16 and 17)

SECOND CATECHESIS

SIN

“Sin is an offense against God: ‘Against you, you only, have I sinned, and done what is evil in your sight’ (Psalm 51:6)

Sin sets itself against God’s love for us and turns our hearts away from it. Like the first sin, it is disobedience, a rebellion against God, through the desire to become ‘like God’ (Genesis 3:5), knowing and determining good and evil. Sin is thus ‘love of oneself even to contempt of God.’”

(Catechism of the Catholic Church, no. 1850)

How is it possible that the holy God, who made himself known as a tender “ally” close to everyone who calls upon him (Deuteronomy 4:7, 32-34), support and guide of the poor, of the outcast (Isaiah 35:1-6 and Judith 9:11), who constantly invites man, with such concern, to transcend himself, to become the precious and beloved image of this merciful fatherhood; how is it possible that such a God should not be welcomed?

That his invitation should be despised?

How can man, who is freely inclined to choose and to want what is best for him, refuse so great a good?

Why can he say “no” to a call that would fulfil him completely, beyond his own desires? (Cf. Romans 8:26 and Ephesians 3:20)

There is only one answer, and it is given by… the one who is the “unheeded”! An enemy has seduced man’s freedom (Matthew 13:24-30). A deadly deception has overturned his inner balance.

“A murderer from the beginning” is how Jesus will describe this enemy (John 8:44)! The “devil,” that is, the one who obstructs, who interrupts the dialogue that had begun between God and man. Out of envy he cried out lies, and suspicion was born in man… the desire to think on his own! Rejecting now a “word” that gave him life, and listening instead to… his own word, from that moment man discovered his autonomy, but also his “nakedness”: who am I? What can I do? What is my destiny?

Despising the free will of the Creator, on whom he depended through “bonds of friendship” (Hosea 11:1-6), he will try to assert himself, denying God’s infinite generosity. Taking himself alone as the measure, he will claim to be the sole master of his future. Sin will be the experience of his own incapacity to give himself life… and “death” makes its entrance into the world (Wisdom 2:22-24)!

Man no longer knows what he does or wants. He is scattered, frightened… absurd! A regret, a nostalgia for the good, makes his existence still more bitter, for it now seems abandoned to hostile forces. The experience of rejecting the divine gift will plunge humanity into tragedy… as the account in Genesis (chapter 3) illuminates. Sin will bring about a situation of fear, anguish, death. Man will find himself alone. Not only separated from God, but… from the other (Genesis 3:12); divided within himself (Genesis 3:10). He is sold to this sad power and will find himself a prisoner (Hebrews 2:14-15)!

This bitter fruit, now entered into the world (Romans 5:12), is inherited from birth (Psalm 51:7)! And it will dwell in man’s heart (Romans 7:10 and Mark 7:21-23). Sin will shut man up in a radical incapacity to find again the way of life (Genesis 3:24). He will be a “fugitive,” pursued by his remorse, like Cain, victim of his disordered desires, inherited from his own parents. A slave of envy, of hatred, of fear of his own sin… (Genesis 4:3-16).

Time grows short, then…; the anxiety appears that everything may be, after all, “vanity of vanities” (Ecclesiastes 1:2). Growing old… dying are slaveries that admit no solution. Man will end up abandoning even his own… word! He will no longer think! Better to distract himself, to be carried along by the immediate. Life slips away from him… all that is left is to seize the pleasure that can now be obtained (Wisdom 2:1-9)! When the dialogue with God has died, the dialogue with oneself dies… and the dialogue with others will end. Others, in fact, become only potential enemies who may threaten one’s own “well-being”! Social life becomes a struggle to survive. Consider, for example, Pharaoh’s reaction toward Israel: once welcomed with such gratitude, now seen only as a nightmare to be… eliminated (Exodus 1)!

No certainty, not even for those who have frantically tried to procure it… Everything is changeable, everything inconsistent. Who are we really? Where are we going? How necessary will be that “word” of salvation: “Father, forgive them!” (Luke 23:34). It will destroy sin, man’s tragedy and his defeat!

“I see the good, oh yes!…” – it is enough that I question myself; enough that I dialogue with creation (Romans 1:18-28); that I reflect on myself (Luke 15:17); that in thought I try to return to the source of being: “Where do I come from?” and that image of life, of likeness to the face of God (Genesis 1:26), asserts itself powerfully!…

“I see the good… I certainly desire to live it again… but I no longer have the strength… I discover my incapacity. I am sold to sin, which alone acts and throws me into what I do not want. Wretched and unhappy man, who will deliver me?…” (Cf. Romans 7:14-24). A cry that sinful man continues to raise; but we know that it has found an answer!

(You can read in the Catechism of the Catholic Church nos. 386 ff.; nos. 1846 ff.).

THIRD CATECHESIS

GOD’S MERCY

“Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Romans 7:24).

It is true, this cry has found an answer!

Rebellious, ungrateful man, forgetful of the many blessings received, now that he has been abandoned… to “his own counsel,” or perhaps better: now that his… freedom has been respected, finds himself in despair. He who believed that lie of a needy “god,” busy protecting himself against his creature (Genesis 3:4-5), can now have a unique experience: that God comes looking for him: “Where are you?” (Genesis 3:9). Sovereignly disinterested, because sovereignly perfect, he can only call him again: he wants to give him once more his “word”… Like a mother he turns to him: “Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should have no compassion on the son of her womb?… Behold, I have graven you on the palms of my hands…” (Isaiah 49:15-16).

God does not appear “offended” by that rebellion; on the contrary… He examines whether he himself had not been like a distracted, inattentive mother… But no, he seeks his “child”: his divine womb still keeps the memory of that creature whom he… brought forth out of love alone! No, he will never forget him!

“You hide, Adam, but you are engraved on the palms of my hands!”

Those hands which one day will physically be nailed to a cross, to make visible how much man is loved with all one’s strength by a divine heart that is also… a mother’s heart!

Zechariah will open his mouth again solely to proclaim this… “tender mercy.” A divine “womb” that brings the sinner to birth anew (Luke 1:68-79)!

God’s motherly care will keep constant watch over the anguished journey of that “son” who wanted to make his own experience, far from the Father’s house. That son will then know famine and hunger. No one will feed him, no one will care about him… The Father, on the other hand, will tremble for him; moved, he will run to meet him, throw himself on his neck, kiss him… as soon as that son “comes to himself,” he will remember that he is a “son,” loved by a Father (Luke 15:11-32). But that Father had been solicitous also toward that other son, Adam, who likewise was anxious and jealous for his own “autonomy.” With gentleness he had made for him “garments of skins” to clothe his “nakedness” (Genesis 3:21); and again, he wished to shield another son, Cain, though a murderer, from the vengeance of his enemies (Genesis 4:15); he wished to preserve them all from the universal corruption (Genesis 6:5-8).

Finally he will choose a poor and barren son, Abraham, so that he may become once again a sign of blessing for all the nations of the earth (Genesis 12:1-3). He will not rest when he hears the cry of pain of these children and sees their oppression at the hands of their enemies (Exodus 3:7-9). He will have to correct their continual relapses with a humiliating exile (Ezekiel 24:15-27), but one that will precede a new and more consoling “exodus” (Isaiah 40:1-11).

The history of salvation is precisely the history of God’s “mercy,” of this gentle and patient love that does not let itself be overcome by evil (Romans 12:21), but conquers by tirelessly granting the possibility of… being born anew: forgiveness! (Hosea 2).

(To understand God’s “tenderness,” you can read: Hosea 11:7-9; Isaiah 41:8-20; Isaiah 43:1 ff.; Isaiah 54:6-10; Psalm 103 and no. 210 of the Catechism of the Catholic Church).

FOURTH CATECHESIS

THE COMPASSION OF JESUS

Jesus is the concrete manifestation, the true face of God’s mercy, of his tenderness, of his love: “He who has seen me has seen the Father” (Cf. John 14:9). God’s “com-passion” led him to love man to the extreme consequences: “God so loved the world that he gave his only Son!” (Cf. John 3:16). And Jesus shared in and collabourated with this marvelous work of the Father: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men… he humbled himself and became obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:6-8). The mission of Jesus is clear: he came to earth, he became one of us, he took on our very nature, so that we might experience his “passion” for us, having shared our history in everything (… except sin!). Born in extreme poverty: “in a cave” (Cf. Luke 2:7); he lived in silence for thirty years at Nazareth, subject to his parents (Cf. Luke 2:51). When he begins his public mission, we find him at once beside the many human miseries, moral and physical. He will be a patient and tireless teacher; he will listen with caring attention; he will bend down in compassion to heal countless wounds; he will welcome with kindness every sort of sinner, giving forgiveness and peace of heart. For all he will become… food of hope, of liberation, of life. In his attitudes the desire of the Father is made present: to be with his people, close to their journey!

“I will never forget you!” God had protested to his people through the prophet Isaiah… and with this motherly tenderness, God’s mercy accompanies our life.

“When a woman is in labor she has pain, because her hour has come; but when she is delivered of the child, she no longer remembers the anguish, for joy that a child is born into the world…” (John 16:21). In this way we can contemplate Jesus’ “com-passion”!

God, from on high, will bend down over man and suffer the pangs of childbirth, to give him life again!

Contemplating this merciful visit of “the dayspring from on high” (Luke 1:78), Zechariah had rejoiced: “… the former troubles are forgotten, the sorrows of old. For behold, God creates new heavens and a new earth, and the former things shall not be remembered, for there will be joy and gladness forever…” (Isaiah 65:17-18).

It is Jesus, therefore, who is the… “new creation,” the motherly face of divine tenderness: “When he saw the crowds, he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless…” (Matthew 9:36). He wants to touch the deep wounds of a weary and burdened humanity: “Come to me, all who labor… and you will find rest” (Matthew 11:28-29). Certainly rest for sinners, dead to love! (Cf. Romans 5:8). For he loved us to the end (John 13:1), sitting at our table (Matthew 9:10-13), bending at our feet to wash and dry them (John 13:5), doing us good… healing us from all those diabolical powers in whose slavery we were held (Acts 10:38)!

Yes, we find rest only in the one who made grace overflow where sin abounded! (Romans 5:18-21); who made himself “neighbor,” like the attentive and caring Samaritan (Luke 10:29 ff.). We can now find rest on the shoulders of the good shepherd who gave his life for us, the sheep (John 10:11) who had gone astray (Luke 15:4-5).

“Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?” (Romans 8:35). “As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you; abide in my love” (John 15:9). To abide in his love, yes, is the experience we are invited to have by the one who loves us, who desires to eat the Passover with us in order to let us experience the joy of passing from creatures dead through sin to new creatures, made in his image… in the image of the Risen One! “I am the resurrection and the life; he who believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live, and whoever lives and believes in me shall never die” (John 11:25-26).

If the innocent Adam once refused this love… the sinner Adam, afflicted and a pilgrim on an earth cursed because of him (Genesis 3:17-19), will find at his side, now and once again, the one who… ardently and from always has sought him and desired him near (Cf. Luke 22:14-15)… at his table (Revelation 3:20)!

“Very good” was that creation… Even more marvelous is “the day which the Lord has made” (Psalm 118:24): the victory of Jesus over sin: our redemption!

This is what the Church sings exultantly at the Easter Vigil: “O happy fault, that earned so great, so glorious a Redeemer!”

The prophecy of Ezekiel, too, finds fulfilment: that immense plain of dry bones receives a word of life: “Prophesy, son of man, say to them: O dry bones, hear the word of the Lord: you shall live!… Say: behold, I will open your graves, and raise you from your graves, O my people. And you shall know that I am the Lord, when I open your graves and raise you from your graves!” (Chapter 37)

Jesus, who died for the sin of the world, was raised for our justification (Romans 3:23-26)… “the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live!” (John 5:25)

Blessed are we, invited to the supper of the Lamb!

(You can read in the Catechism of the Catholic Church nos. 1503, 2448, 2575, 2715.)

FIFTH CATECHESIS

THE NECESSITY OF PRAYER

“This great nation is a wise and understanding people. For what great nation is there that has a god so near to it as the Lord our God is to us, whenever we call upon him?” (Deuteronomy 4:7).

The God who reveals himself draws near to man’s needs

Israel’s experience was that of becoming an intelligent, wise, rich, free people… a great nation, because it had been saved by God’s intervention, who made himself the “ally” of a… mass of powerless and desperate slaves. And the God of Israel will remain close to this people, saving it from all the historical situations in which it will find itself trapped and in which it will risk being lost: “In your distress, in the latter days, you will return to the Lord your God and obey his voice, for the Lord your God is a merciful God; he will not fail you or destroy you or forget the covenant with your fathers which he swore to them” (Deuteronomy 4:30-31).

“Call upon me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me” (Psalm 50:15).

Always the God of Israel, who revealed himself to Abraham, to Isaac, to Jacob, has been sensitive to this cry of anguish: “In distress you called, and I delivered you; I answered you in the secret place of thunder” (Psalm 81:7).

He draws near though infinitely far away, because he loves man

Vital appears this “cry” of man rising up to God, to obtain liberation, life, happiness.

“Wrapped in the cloud” of the mystery of his transcendent, holy, eternal existence… and yet God is so near, so attentive, every time man calls upon him. This is what Israel learned in its history: “Give thanks to the Lord, call upon his name; make known his deeds among the nations” (Isaiah 12:4).

And he begins to speak to him…

Israel, the Patriarchs themselves, knew a God who… converses, who wants to speak, who awaits a reply. “Hear, O my people, while I admonish you! O Israel, if you would but listen to me! Open your mouth wide and I will fill it… O that my people would listen to me… I would soon subdue their foes” (Psalm 81:8-14).

…from person to person.

A “personal” God… “eager” to communicate, to give, to lead man to rest. Because he knows his creature… “He who planted the ear, does he not hear? He who formed the eye, does he not see?” (Psalm 94:9). God wanted man, loves him… “The Lord set his love upon you and chose you, not because you were more in number than any other people – for you were the fewest of all peoples – but because the Lord loves you” (Deuteronomy 7:7-8). Without God, man no longer finds his very… being: “The Lord knows the thoughts of man, that they are but a breath” (Psalm 94:11); “If the Lord had not been my help, my soul would soon have dwelt in the land of silence” (Psalm 94:17).

Called to account by God, man comes to know who he is.

Created in the “image and likeness” of God, man fulfils his own existence in communion with the other. He needs the other in order to converse; he wants to be listened to… loved! Man’s being is fulfilled in a relationship of “communion.”

Man is the image of God. God reveals himself as “Trinity”: communion of persons.

But this need of man is what it is because he was created by God and willed by God in his own image: the divine nature itself is, in fact, “communion”! The inner life of God is made up of the “eternal dialogue” that takes place in the depths of love between the Father and the Son. For man too, then, the fullness of being, and therefore of love, can only be consummated in a personal relationship with the other. Only with God, certainly, does it become absolute and fulfilling.

The pedagogy of divine revelation

God reveals to man this need for listening and for invocation in order to introduce him into that mystery of life which will constitute man’s eternal beatitude: “He shall cry to me: ‘You are my Father, my God, and the Rock of my salvation’” (Psalm 89:26).

“Do not be silent to me, O my God, lest, if you be silent to me, I become like those who go down to the pit” (Psalm 28:1).

To reveal himself is a sign of communion, of the gift of self.

When he speaks, God gives himself to man in order to invite him to do the same: man, by calling upon God and opening himself to dialogue, learns to give himself, to know God, to communicate with him and to become… like him! “I cry to God Most High, to God who fulfills his purpose for me” (Psalm 57:2).

God is man’s supreme good!

Yes, God “does good” to man, and therefore it is necessary that man seek God, welcome his word, desire his communion: “O God, you are my God, my soul thirsts for you” (Psalm 63:1), “When shall I come and behold the face of God?” (Psalm 42-43:2).

It is necessary for man to “meet” God.

This need for man to welcome the divine invitation and begin the dialogue that will lead him to the experience of meeting his God is also emphasised by Saint Paul: “No one who believes in him will be put to shame. For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; the same Lord is Lord of all and bestows his riches upon all who call upon him. For, ‘everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved’” (Romans 10:11-13). As for Israel, so for every man salvation is possible when man discovers the need to have close to him that God who kindly wishes to establish with him a relationship of communion.

From Israel, precisely, we must learn the necessity of prayer: “Take no rest, and give him no rest…” (Isaiah 62:6-7). For us too, those expressions would become true and timely: “do not keep silence or be still,” “do not be far from me,” “rouse yourself, awake, show yourself,” “stir up your might,” “arise and go to your resting place.” Yes, O Lord, do not remain silent or still before our miseries: “Do not keep silence, O God!” (Psalm 83:1). Bring us to your rest! “Rise up, come to our help!” (Psalm 44:26).

But sin… has interrupted that dialogue with God

The bitter experience of sin (Romans 5:17-18, 20-23): that wearisome pilgrimage through life (Genesis 3:16-19), made so often of painful separations, of deadly loneliness; and then having come to know, in this tragedy, that someone has drawn near, not merely to console superficially, but to heal and wholly renew our reality, transfiguring it and even exalting it beyond death, are events that certainly provoke contradictory reactions: of sorrow and anguish at first, but finally of wonder, amazement, hope…

If a gravely ill person discovers that a famous physician can diagnose the virus that is killing him and give him a therapy that will lead him to recovery, surely that person will want to get in touch with that physician…

Our life has known, or will know, disappointments, failures, difficulties of every kind: exasperating selfishness, injustices and oppressions, hatreds and divisions, the unleashing of passions… problems that all too often admit no solution (Matthew 24:6-8 and Luke 21:8-19). “Sin entered into the world” (Romans 5:12) and brought forth death! But into this world God’s mercy has also entered: “Fear not!…” (John 12:31 and 16:33). If God has made himself a strong ally of our weaknesses and our incapacities, then crying out to him, seeking him anxiously, will become a fundamental need of our life: let us say it plainly, a matter of life or death!

Now it becomes necessary… to “give back”!

This necessity of prayer, of asking, that is, with insistence and trust, is what Jesus has revealed to us. He himself, first of all, prayed often (Luke 5:16; 9:18, 29; 11:1)… whole nights (Luke 6:12); every day, moreover, he faithfully went to the Temple (Luke 22:53 and John 8:2) and on the sabbath to the synagogue (Mark 1:21; 3:1; 6:2; Luke 4:16 and John 18:20). In the dramatic moment of Gethsemane, when his soul groaned in the anguish of the trial, we are told that he prayed more earnestly (Luke 22:44). Not only that: according to what the letter to the Hebrews reveals (5:7), throughout his earthly life Jesus offered up to God loud cries and tears! Surely because of the situation with which he stood in solidarity: our humanity separated from God! Truly the wages of sin was death (Romans 6:23)! And the death from which Jesus asks to be delivered is certainly not the physical one (for which, as we know, he was not heard!).

“My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Psalm 22:1), cried out on the cross, is our cry: the despair of the whole of humanity on the brink of an endless existential tragedy! Indeed, man’s failure is grave and goes beyond death (Matthew 25:31-46); it calls for an… impossible thing (Luke 18:26-27), a divine intervention that gives an answer, that saves, that justifies! “It is true, I have sinned against you – prays the psalmist – but you, deliver me and save me!” (Cf. Psalm 51).

Jesus, the innocent, the just one, will take our place and from that… depth of death (Psalm 130), he will cry out and… be heard. Because of his piety.

Hence the necessity of… piety: that merciful love of God who gives us his Son and who awaits a filial obedience.

Jesus, the obedient son and faithful servant, “faithfully brought forth” that “justice” which we had lost: to be obedient sons and daughters! All of us, from desperate loneliness, were waiting for such a… “teaching” (Isaiah 42:1-4)!

The vital importance, therefore, of Jesus’ witness

Now, “God’s love has been poured into our hearts” (Romans 5:5) and we can cry: “Abba! Father!” (Romans 8:15).

The witness of Jesus’ whole life reminds us, therefore, of the need and urgency of prayer: of asking, of seeking, of knocking (Luke 11:9) with insistence (Luke 11:5-8), aware of our unworthiness (Luke 18:9-14) and of our poverty (Luke 18:1-8); importunate, certainly, but… at last sons and daughters!

The teaching of the apostles will also reflect what they learned from their Master: here and there, in the letters, they hand on to us prayers, especially of praise and thanksgiving; they too recommend perseverance and constancy in prayer to the Holy Spirit, addressed to God through Christ. They speak to us of its great effectiveness for sanctification and do not fail to recall the prayer of praise, thanksgiving, petition and intercession for all (Romans 8:15, 26; 12:12;

1 Corinthians 12:3; Galatians 4:6; 2 Corinthians 1:20; Colossians 3:17; 4:2;

Hebrews 13:15; Ephesians 6:18; 1 Timothy 4:5; 1 John 3:22; James 5:14, 16).

An asking day and night, then, without growing weary; so as not to risk falling back into the original temptation (Matthew 26:41-42), that of the “fool” who says in his heart: “There is no God!” (Psalm 14).

SIXTH CATECHESIS

IN THE PRAYER OF THE POOR

The apostolic Church kept that command of Jesus: “Watch, that you may not enter into temptation” (Matthew 26:41) and: “ask in my name to obtain from the Father…” (John 15:16 and 16:24). Right after Pentecost, in fact, Peter would understand what the mission of the “Twelve” was to be: to proclaim the “good news” of the victory of the Risen Lord and to remain in communion with him through “unceasing” prayer (1 Thessalonians 5:17 and Acts 6:4). The Acts of the Apostles bears witness to how faithful the Apostles were to liturgical prayer: they frequented the Temple at the various hours of the day, until, like Jesus, they began to suffer persecution at the hands of the Sanhedrin (Acts 2:46; 3:1; 5:20; 21:26). The prayer of the Apostles, like the prayer Jesus himself had prayed, had its roots in the “word of God”. God himself, in fact, had given not only the way to address him but had also revealed the feelings and states of mind that his people would experience in their history.

God, that is, teaches man to know himself, to feel what stirs him and what troubles him; why he yields to despair or why, or over what, he rejoices. At the same time he suggests to man that he, the saving God, is at his side, knows how to listen to him, wants to help him, is ready to intervene… The whole pedagogy of God in revealing himself as a “faithful ally”, precious and indispensable to man, is narrated in the book of PSALMS.

The Psalms: prayer given by God to man. God… “lends” prayer to man!

They above all give us the interior life of Jesus. He himself had reminded his disciples that the Psalms too, besides the Law and the Prophets, had written what concerned his life, his feelings, his mission (Luke 24:44).

God reveals the dramatic situation of man (Gen 3)

The situation of man (we have already seen it) is grave: there is an infernal enemy who has brought into the world despair, hatred, every form of violence, death! And man lives in this slavery of unhappiness: humiliated, poor, weak, alone!

Jesus takes on this condition… Here, then, is that prayer “with loud cries and tears” (Hebrews 5:7): from that situation of death which distresses. “In my distress I called upon the Lord… in my anguish I cried out, he rescued me from powerful enemies, stronger than I” (Psalm 18:7, 19). “I lie down among lions that devour” (Psalm 57:5). “If the Lord had not been with us, they would have swallowed us alive” (Psalm 124:2-3). “I cry aloud for help… I plead… I pour out my complaint… while my spirit faints” (Psalm 142:2-4).

That is why God, loving man, makes himself… close to him!

The psalms are there to point out the enemies concretely: the powerful, the exploiters, the rich, slanderers, deceivers… In short, the “wicked”! Who lie in wait for the life of the man who longs for “salvation”: “turn to me… I am alone and wretched… see my enemies… many hate me” (Psalm 25:16, 19); “come to save me, come quickly to my aid” (Psalm 70:2); “answer me, for I am poor and wretched… in the day of my distress I lift my cry to you” (Psalm 86:1, 7); “… my heart is wounded within me” (Psalm 109:22).

But who is the wicked man?

The psalms define as such the man who thinks: “There is no God” (Psalm 53:2) or “God is not there” (Psalm 14:1).

To deny every search for God, or the need to enter into communion with the absolute, becomes for man… folly! The “fool” is therefore the man who considers the need for prayer absurd or meaningless: “God does not care; there is no God” (Psalm 10:4), “how could God know? Is there knowledge in the Most High?” (Psalm 73:11).

The wicked man does not know himself; he does not understand how much his being is “dependent” on everything and everyone. He does not perceive the deep meaning of life, of his future. He does not know that, in order to “grow”, to establish himself, he constantly needs help, needs to receive… “grace upon grace” (John 1:16)!

Let us see how the psalms portray this “foolish” man: the wicked one!

Such precisely because “not pious”. Jesus, on the contrary, was heard and delivered from death because of his piety!

The wicked man does not set God before himself (Psalm 54:5). He neither wants nor seeks, therefore, this relationship. Rather, he denies it. He accuses the righteous man who bears witness to it, and insults him: “Where is your God?” (Psalm 42:4). He lifts his head against heaven (Psalm 75:6). His pride leads him to boast of what he does: “the venom of vipers is under their lips” (Psalm 140:3): arrogance, deceit, quarrels, malice, envy, violence, evil thoughts, iniquity, malicious speech, plunder… (Psalms 52; 56; 73)

He delights, moreover, in lying: apparently speaking well of the other, but judging him inwardly, “plotting only to bring him down” (Psalm 62:5). If he makes an agreement, it is only to hide traps (Psalm 64:6); he even conspires to strike the innocent in secret. He strikes by surprise, without feeling remorse (Psalm 64:5).

The habitual attitudes of the wicked man: he makes a din; he pursues with fury; he shouts; he never ceases to provoke abuse (Psalm 55:4, 12).

In what does he trust? In his “great wealth”, which he calmly goes on “heaping up” (Psalm 52:9; 73:12), ignoring the affliction of others… For him there is no suffering: he enjoys prosperity and success (Psalm 73:3-5). Moreover, he trusts in power. Not to govern with uprightness, but to plot violence (Psalm 58:2-3), or even to influence the judgments of rulers and thus oppress the poor, the weak, the needy (Psalm 82:2-4).

He can, therefore, boast of a dominion all his own, unchallenged.

He can act insolently with impunity and even kill widows, strangers and orphans (Psalm 94:3-7).

But the wonders of God are hope of “liberation” and, therefore, the foundation of prayer!

If the wicked man “hates discipline and casts God’s words behind him” (Psalm 50:16-17), the devout man, even while acknowledging himself a sinner, meditates “day and night” on the wonders of God (Psalm 1:2). He needs to hear them “told” (Psalm 44:2-4) in order to hope in salvation (Psalm 35:3). “The senseless man”, on the other hand, “does not know, and the fool does not understand” (Psalm 92:6).

Mary, in the “Magnificat”, will be able to rejoice in God “her Savior” because she kept in her heart those great things which the Holy One, from generation to generation, has done to help Israel and to remember the mercy promised to the fathers.

This “meditating” on the works of God makes… “clean”!

Just like the apostles, who were witnesses of all the signs Jesus performed (John 15:3). Though sinners, though in need of redemption… yet they persevered (Luke 22:28). Remaining in Jerusalem awaiting a “power” (Acts 1:4, 8). The whole of Psalm 119, for example, is a song of praise and thanksgiving for this divine gift of salvation, for the word that comes to light up the dark paths of the human heart. Waiting for this power prepares one to fight against despair, against the night of evil. “It is good to give thanks to the Lord, to sing praise to your name, O Most High, to proclaim your love in the morning and your faithfulness by night… For you make me glad, O Lord, by your deeds!” (Psalm 92:2-3, 5).

The teachings of Jesus too will insist on “watching” and “praying at all times” in order to have the “strength”, from God, to escape all that is about to happen of… the dramatic! (Luke 21:34-36).

And meditation on the wonders of God becomes supplication, a call for help, a plea for forgiveness

Frequent, then, will be the attitudes of the righteous man who laments, who sighs, who pleads: “I cry aloud to God and he hears me”… “in the day of my distress I lift my cry to you”… “my eyes are ever on the Lord”… “I am restless in my complaint”… “let the groans of the prisoners come before you”… “my eyes fail from weeping… you have counted my wanderings”… “do not turn a deaf ear to my plea”… “come quickly to set me free”…

If the enemies are fierce, his soul will appear troubled (Psalm 6:3-4). Prayer will become invocation and cry for help (Psalm 22:2-3). Through the experience of his own weakness, through the situation of evil common to all men, the righteous man will discover prayer as a humble plea for forgiveness (Psalm 51). Prayer, in all its different states of mind, will keep the righteous man watchful: it will become his only comfort, his incentive to hope. An example, in Psalms 77 and 102.

…but above all the need to persevere in prayer!

In the righteous man, now, there is the… need for prayer: “in the morning I call to you and wait” (Psalm 5:4)… “at daybreak I seek you… my flesh longs for you” (Psalm 63:2)… “evening, morning and noon I cry out” (Psalm 55:17-18)… “because of my loud groaning” (Psalm 102:6)… “my soul waits for the Lord” (Psalm 130:6).

A need to wait, therefore, to hope: the enemies always trample; many are those who oppress (Psalm 56:2-3). The insult is daily (Psalm 42:4, 11); God seems… almost distant (Psalm 9/10:22).

“How long?…”

This “cry” reveals even more the situation of unbearable hardship (Psalm 13:2-3).

And yet the righteous man does not cease to hope (Psalm 71:14), to send up to God his unceasing prayer (Psalms 57:2-3; 77:2; 102:2-3; 123:2). He must learn to trust: “my soul finds rest in God alone” (Psalm 62:2). He can, therefore, abandon himself to God’s faithfulness (Psalm 52:10); he can hope in him (Psalm 42:12), because God will set him free (Psalm 81:8) and make him dwell in the land (Psalm 37:29).

Prayer that becomes song, praise and blessing

Help can come from him alone (Psalm 121:1-2) and only he can work those wonders that make us rejoice (Psalms 40:4, 6; 46:9; 75:2; 77:12-13; 78:6-7), above all the “poor” (Psalms 12:6; 102:18-22)! Prayer then becomes exaltation of divine power and greatness (Psalms 95:1-5; 100:4-5; 105:1-4). The wicked man already vanishes and the glory of the living God is revealed (Psalm 138:3-8). God, in fact, laughs at all the mighty who fight against him (Psalms 2:4; 37:13). Power belongs to him (Psalm 62:12); he decides the cases of the peoples (Psalm 7:9) and threatens the nations (Psalm 33:10). God alone does what he wills in heaven and on earth (Psalms 24:1-2; 33:6; 95:4; 135:6): he is King forever! (Psalms

47:3, 8; 89:9; 90:2; 145:1-3).

The heavens tell of his glory (Psalms 19:2; 89:6) and above the heavens his majesty is raised (Psalm 8:2); his paths are truth and grace (Psalms 25:10; 36:8, 10). He guides his people (Psalm 48:15), saves men and animals (Psalm 36:7), delivers from distress (Psalms 4:2; 107:6), brings back the exiles (Psalm 85:2), forgives, heals, satisfies, renews (Psalms 103:3-5; 146:7-10), keeps watch (Psalm 12:8), does not abandon his people (Psalm 94:14), restores life (Psalm 138:7), protects the city (Psalm 127:1)!

God is creator (Psalm 104) and Lord of history (Psalms 78:12-16; 105; 106); he has his dwelling in Jerusalem (Psalms 76:3; 147:2), gives joy there (Psalm 122:1-4), because lovely are his dwelling places (Psalm 84:2-3). He is Father (Psalms 68:6; 103:13), he knows, therefore, the human heart (Psalm 139); he can, for this reason, forgive (Psalms 65:3-4; 103:3) and wrap all in his tenderness (Psalms 69:17; 111:4; 145:9).

In the morning invocation, the figure of old Zechariah looms large: his priestly tongue, paralyzed by unbelief, by disappointments, by the barren sunset of life, opens again in praise, embracing that unexpected son, yet longed for through very many years! “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people… he has raised up for us a mighty salvation… he has shown mercy and remembered his holy covenant… to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Luke 1:68-79)

Because God is the shepherd (Psalm 23) who lets nothing be lacking. He, the “rock”, the “fortress”, the “deliverer”, “shield and stronghold”, “mighty salvation”: it is enough to call upon him and the enemies are defeated! (Psalm 18).

He will give strength to his people (Psalm 29:11), will bow the heavens and come down (Psalm 18:10), will make his face shine (Psalm 80:4), will give joy and great gladness (Psalm 70:5)… who is like the Lord? (Psalms 89:9; 113:5-6): for his everlasting mercy (Psalms 100:5; 136), for his faithfulness (Psalms 52:10; 91:5), for the depth of his thoughts (Psalm 92:6), HE IS WORTHY OF PRAISE! (Psalm 96:4).

Even in a violent and corrupt world, he continues to bend down over men (Psalm 53:3); he does not keep silent (Psalm 50:3); he continues to inspire good in the hearts of sinners (Psalm 51:8). His grace must therefore be sought (Psalm 63:4) and man at last discovers that he is a “wonder”! (Psalm 71:6-7). The righteous man can therefore rejoice in the day the Lord has made for him (Psalm 118:24): that resurrection to which continual and trusting prayer has led him (Psalms 9:11; 25:2; 32:10).

Prayer becomes necessary as… the “Passover”!

Like the Passover, then, the path of prayer is necessarily marked by stages: painful slaveries, deadly anguish, numerous and violent enemies… then the benevolent and loving intervention of God and then… it becomes possible to “go out” into freedom, life, peace!

Precisely in that prayer, become a song of praise, in which man can rejoice in the knowledge and… possession of God, all human toil comes to an end and the history of humanity finds its fulfilment!

Truly great, then, is man! Truly a wonder. Created to be little less than a “god”. “Give God no rest”: Isaiah was right to announce to Israel that it should never forget the divine promises (Isaiah 62:6-7). That people had understood how vital and necessary is the relationship of unceasing dialogue with that God who had sworn to be their ally forever!

Every psalm bears witness to the need for prayer!

Prayer is therefore a paschal journey: from darkness to light, from despair to joy, from painful groaning to the song of praise. It is the journey lived by Israel. The journey of every man. A journey necessary in order to “enter” into life. But like every journey, to bear fruit it must be persevering. It remains only to point out how the psalms help us to verify this continually. Precisely in the two psalms that… open the Psalter, all this appears evident: in Psalm 1, happiness is acquired by meditating on the Law of God day and night. Trusting perseverance will bear fruit in its season.

In Psalm 2, prayer is necessary to obtain divine sonship! Clear is the divine invitation: “Ask of me, and I will give…” A journey with a wonderful promise. Confirmed by Psalm 110: “Sit at my right hand”.

Prayer will make the desire to dwell in God’s sanctuary grow (Psalms 15; 65; 84; 122); it will be necessary to overcome trials (Psalms 17; 89; 141; 146); to obtain what we deeply desire:

life and the savoring of its sweetness (Psalms 27; 128); to rejoice with gladness (Psalm 31); to learn wisdom (Psalm 90); to receive peace (Psalm 116); to be freed from eternal misery (Psalm 28); to experience divine providence (Psalms 34; 35; 94; 144; 145); to welcome forgiveness (Psalms 32; 51; 130); to learn to be merciful (Psalm 82); not to fall into discouragement (Psalms 60; 61; 95); to arrive, finally, at praise (Psalms 103; 104; 105; 106; 107; 139; 147; 148)

It is in the prayer of praise, in fact, that the greatness of man is manifested: see Psalm 8 and note further, in Psalm 18, how only in this prayer does man find his security. Not by chance, precisely at the end of the Psalter, the songs of joy and blessing to God are more numerous, as the conclusion of a journey that leads man, through prayer, to contemplate the face of his God (Psalms 19; 24; 36; 45; 98; 100; 118).

It is the only book of Scripture, the Psalter (“Liturgy of the Hours”), that the Church gives us as a book of prayer. If man fulfils himself in communion with the other, prayer, which opens the dialogue between God and man, will be for him the vital, supreme, necessary relationship… With this “word” man can express himself and reach his perfection, a… fullness of life!

Blessed is that soul who can experience this providential care of his God and acclaim him, walking in the light of his face! (Psalm 89:16). The light that enveloped the whole universe, from the beginning, tears through the darkness and opens the horizon to new life: “You show me the path of life, fullness of joy in your presence; you will not abandon my life to the grave, nor let your holy one see corruption!” (Psalm 16:10-11).

FOR THE NEXT STAGES OF THE JOURNEY

Once the catecheses indicated have been completed (which need not necessarily be carried out in only six meetings…), the brothers will be invited to live the experience of psalm prayer, the prayer… of the poor, in order to begin to discover the validity of their own call to belong to the

Movement of Hope which, “through the Holy Mother of Mary, are rooted in the spirituality of the poor of Yahweh” (Statute no. 14)

To understand better the value of this prayer, which is moreover inspired by God, it will be fitting to read what the Magisterium teaches in the Apostolic Constitution on the Liturgy of the Hours, by Paul VI.

Together with prayer, it is hoped that in this same period the brothers will be initiated into familiarity with the Bible: both materially, getting to know its composition (the sacred books of the Old and New Testaments), but in a very simple way, and at a more spiritual level, learning the historical events of the people of Israel that gave rise to our spirituality. A history of… poor people, that of Israel, yet it was the womb in which Jesus would live his own history, giving us the way of salvation and the right to call ourselves again, and to be… “children of God!”

To make the start easier for you…, we have thought of preparing for you ourselves a brief summary of this history, pointing out some readings that we consider most significant.

THE PATRIARCHS

From the call of Abraham (about 1850 BC) to the entry into Egypt (1700 BC).

The history of salvation is a history of poor people. Men who have known suffering, disappointments, persecutions of various kinds, failures and anguish. The God who reveals himself in this history is a personal and unique God who enters into relationship with the lives of these… poor men!

ABRAHAM

We could say that biblical history begins with Abraham. This rich nomad is 75 years old, but childless. If God appears to him promising: “I will make of you a great nation”, we may believe that this was Abraham’s anguish throughout his life: a barren wife (Genesis 11:30), a future without descendants. Now, after that mysterious encounter, Abraham must lean on that “word” and must… set out (Genesis 12). He will have difficulties of various kinds: natural ones, such as famine, misunderstandings and fears on the part of foreigners, quarrels with relatives (Genesis 13), tribal wars (Genesis 14).

Moreover: that God who seems to fall silent for long periods and who puts Abraham’s faith in crisis:

“The heir of my house will be a servant of mine!”

Slowly, instead, God goes on revealing his gift: “One born of you shall be your heir” (Genesis 15).

But Abraham’s understanding is still imperfect: perhaps from a slave woman he may have children…

Again suffering and confusion will come to man from continuing to believe that something good can happen by his own will (Genesis 16). God’s fidelity to his chosen one will be Abraham’s only consolation: “I will make you exceedingly numerous” (Genesis 17). Finally the fulfilment of the promise: “Sarah, your wife, will bear you a son” (Genesis 17:19).

THE DIVINE IMPOSSIBLE NOW ENTERS THE HISTORY OF THE POOR!

This experience will change Abraham’s life. He is now sure of this covenant, which rests only on God’s promise (Genesis 15:17). Abraham will have to believe in this strong intimacy of his God, who wants to free him from every anguish and give him a happiness greater than his own expectations. So deeply rooted is his trust that, when God tests him by asking for his son, Abraham will not doubt (Genesis 22). Though not understanding how God will provide, nevertheless he will not… waver! Isaac will be the living sign of his God who gave him to him, from a barren woman!

God will provide, then, even for death!

Abraham is no longer afraid. We can note the gentleness of the Patriarch, formed by this God, in the episode with his nephew Lot: he accepts that the young man choose for himself the… best (humanly speaking!). On returning from the victory over the four kings, he will not claim… the rights of war (Genesis 14:23). Respectful and humble, again, in his meeting with Melchizedek. Though rich in promises, he is aware of being a pilgrim in that land which only in the future will belong to his descendants; so he will buy of it only as much as is needed to bury Sarah (Genesis 23).

But great will be the trusting openness of his heart to God when he intercedes for Sodom (Genesis 18). His insistent and trusting prayer will save Lot (Genesis 19:1-29).

ISAAC

He is the son of joy: longed for, yet obtained by God’s miraculous intervention!

Obedient, gentle, loving toward his parents, he will inherit the divine “blessing” (Genesis 25:5).

Abraham will take care that he never return to the land of origin, so that he may go on dwelling in the place God has shown him. He will obtain for him as a wife Rebekah, who will console him for the loss of his mother (Genesis 24). He will have a deep devotion to his father’s God, and soon he will become his own God. He will plead with him over his wife’s barrenness (Genesis 25:21); he will listen to him when he tells him where to go to protect himself from famine (Genesis 26:1-2).

Note: Isaac is a peaceful and patient man. He bears the envy of his neighbours, accepts their violence… yielding and finally forgiving, reconciling himself with those who had despised him (Genesis 26:12-31).

JACOB

The name underlines his… future: “the one who supplants” or, perhaps: “may God protect.” Indeed, he will supplant his brother in the right of the firstborn, which Esau, exhausted from work, will sell to Jacob… out of hunger (Genesis 25:29-34)! But it is also true that God will protect Jacob, making use of Rebekah and letting him obtain the divine “blessing” which from Isaac should have passed, as a sacred inheritance, to Esau (Genesis 27), had he not, with too much superficiality, despised that birthright, exchanging it for a more immediate and tangible good!

Jacob will have to flee from Esau’s wrath, but God will continue to protect his chosen one (Genesis 28).

He will be humbled and will work hard in a… foreign land, in the house of his uncle Laban; but he will grow rich in children and, by cunning, in possessions too (Genesis 30), so much so that he withdraws… prudently even from his uncle (Genesis 31:17-29). After so many years, Jacob still dreads the meeting with Esau, but God will protect him again. After a night of solitude and mysterious struggle with God, Jacob will wrest the definitive blessing: his name will be changed to Israel, that is: “you have been strong with God” (Genesis 32). That dreaded meeting with Esau… will turn into reconciliation (Genesis 33:1-4).

Now God will commit himself to defending this man and all his descendants. This does not prevent the Patriarchs, and later the people, from often falling into very grave sins: an example in chapter 34. The blessing of Abraham, moreover, will not be able to descend upon the firstborn Reuben, because of his sin of incest (Genesis 35:22), nor upon Simeon and Levi, violent and vindictive. Judah, the fourth son, will be the heir of the birthright.

From this family, later, David will be born and then, in the fullness of time, Jesus.

JOSEPH

He is Jacob’s most beloved son (Genesis 37:3), born of his most beloved wife: Rachel. Yet Joseph will have to suffer much! Hated by his brothers, sold as a slave, far from his father’s affection and from his own land, he will suffer every sort of injustice (Genesis 39). The gift of interpreting dreams, however (Genesis 40), will obtain for him freedom from slavery and the trust of Pharaoh (Genesis 41). He will become the man of providence, both for Egypt and… for his brothers (Genesis 42 and 43)!

Though he puts them to the… test (Genesis 44), so that they may become aware of their sin (Genesis 42:21), Joseph in the end will make himself known (Genesis 45) and will forgive from the heart; indeed he will declare that the whole story of pain that their hatred caused him served God to save the family of Jacob (Genesis 50).

Thus, thanks to Joseph, Egypt will welcome with recognition and gratitude those brothers who one day had plotted the death of their present… saviour (Genesis 47:1-6).

With Joseph the history of the Patriarchs closes, and the first book of the Bible. God truly “shows himself strong” with these men, loving them, doing them good and filling them with every blessing… But time passes and man… forgets.

That family grows. Now it is a people.

The book of Exodus opens like the story of Abraham. Israel is no longer a welcome guest: it is under the nightmare of slavery, of death and of its own powerlessness to free itself!

EXODUS (about 1250 BC)

Israel is a slave people but… fruitful.

Egypt, powerful and despotic, is instead… fearful!

God will bless those who bear witness for life (Exodus 1).

And Moses will be saved, to be witness and herald of the “I AM” (Exodus 2). The God of the Fathers who draws near to the groans and sufferings of man. The God of compassion for every slavery, the “ETERNAL PRESENT”, moves history toward unhoped-for liberations, promising and accomplishing sovereign freedoms and dignity without limits (Exodus 3). The most perfect Being, the “I AM WHO I AM”, source and life of every being, does not fear the resistance of the proud, nor the weakness of the poor (Exodus 5:1-9; 7:14-18; 8:1-2; 9:1-3; 10:1-6; 11:1-5).

The force of these divine interventions in history will be fixed definitively in the “memorial” of the Passover: feast of the Lord! He will commit himself, for all generations, to be the “God of the humble, protector of the discouraged, helper of the forsaken, savior of the despairing” (Exodus 12:1-28 and 13:17-22). The attempts of evil to take revenge will be of no avail (Exodus 14:5-31): Pharaoh, figure of every enemy of God and of man, will be destroyed and those redeemed by the Lord will be able to sing the hymn of praise (Exodus [reference incomplete in the original]). Then the mysterious march toward the land of freedom will begin. But how hard the people’s… balking! Unbelieving and doubtful, it too often forgets the wonders of its God, to long for the times of slavery! (Exodus 16:1-3 and 17:1-3). And yet it is with this people that the living God binds himself by an everlasting oath (Exodus 19:3-8; 20 and 24). The building of the “sanctuary” too, which will be in the image of the “heavenly” one (Exodus 25:40), shown in a vision to Moses in his dialogue with God, becomes a visible sign of God’s desire to accompany this people!

God wants to be there, in that “dwelling”, in the midst of that people of his which he has acquired…

Even though the people, impatient and rebellious, soon betray him (Exodus 32). Only Moses, the one chosen for this mission, will pray and plead for forgiveness… (Exodus 33:12-17).

The covenant will be renewed and the journey will resume.

To understand the “holiness” of God, that is, how his intimate life, the manifestation of his will, his very nature were truly given to this ignorant, rough, violent people, grown up for years in oppression, you can read Leviticus 19 and Deuteronomy 5, 6 and 8.

God makes himself an ally in order to educate Israel in holiness. He wants it to become… perfect, as he is!, the living God, who made himself known in order to give life and happiness.

In the book of Numbers, you can read chapters 11:1-9; 16:1-11; 20:1-5 and 21:4-8, to note how the nature of this people, on the contrary, is still far from the desires of its God!

In chapters 13 and 14:1-4, again in Numbers, you can finally understand the reasons for the long wandering in the desert before entering at last the promised land.

JOSHUA (1220 – 1200 BC)

Faithful and obedient to Moses’ guidance, he will agree to lead the people of the new generation into possession of the land. This conquest too will involve struggles and sacrifices. But the Lord, faithful to his promises, will accompany the settlement of the twelve tribes of Israel in Palestine and, once again, will summon his people to offer them his covenant anew (Joshua 24).

JUDGES (1200 – 1025 BC)

They are “charismatic” leaders, raised up by God at moments when Israel, forgetful of the “covenant”, betrays it and experiences its own weakness: it falls into the hands of occasional enemies. Its cry of anguish rises again to God who, moved to pity, provides liberation through these men. They will also show the way to be followed, though not wholly immune from many imperfections: see the fears of Barak (Judges 4:8); the uncertainties of Gideon (Judges 6:36-40 and 7:2-3); the violence of Abimelech (Judges 9:5); the sacrilegious superstition of Jephthah (Judges 11:30-31, 35); the naive imprudence of Samson.

But trust in God, in the end, will triumph over their weakness. Ardent and eager for redemption, for example, the experience of Samson (Judges 16).

SAMUEL (1040 BC)

He is the last great “judge”; he inaugurates, though reluctantly (1 Samuel 8:5-22), the monarchy in Israel, consecrating its first two kings: one, Saul (1 Samuel 10:1-8), rejected by God for his disobedience, and the other, David, pleasing instead to the divine heart (1 Samuel 16:1-13).

DAVID

The first book of Samuel ends with the death of Saul (1 Samuel 31); the second book of Samuel begins with David’s rise to the throne and will tell of his deeds, above all the definitive victory over the Philistines, who had long threatened the independence of the people of Yahweh (2 Samuel 1:1-16; 5:1-12 and 8). But more important, the recovery of the Kingdom after the death of his son Absalom, who, rebelling against his father, had tried to take it from him! David will meet the betrayal of this son of his with meekness and will accept as a… penitential pilgrimage his flight from the holy city (2 Samuel 15:13-37). Even the grief over Absalom’s death will be seen as atonement for his sins of murder and adultery (2 Samuel 19:1-15). David will think of building a magnificent Temple for God. The prophet Nathan, who at first approves, will afterwards bring him God’s answer: the Temple will be built by his son Solomon. But God, who will have appreciated his pious concern, will make David magnificent promises: Israel is established forever as the people of God, governed by the house of David (2 Samuel 7)!

SOLOMON (970 – 931 BC)

He succeeded David in the Kingdom. Famous for his wisdom (often too worldly), for his political activity (conducted more by diplomacy than by arms), for trade, great building projects (royal palace, Temple, various fortifications…), the centralization of administration. His religious sentiment was less deeply rooted than David’s and his worldly concerns excessive. In old age he gave way to idolatry (1 Kings 11:1-8) and, in domestic politics, he exasperated the dualism between north and south, favouring Judah (many of his fellow citizens chosen for high offices of state) and burdening Israel with excessive tributes. This weakness and imprudence of his will lead to the schism (1 Kings 11:26-40).

THE TWO KINGDOMS

After Solomon’s death, Rehoboam will ascend the throne of Judah (931 – 913) who, by his foolish lack of understanding, will provoke the political schism (1 Kings 12:1-25). Israel will divide into two kingdoms: the north, with ten tribes, will keep the name of Israel. Its capital, later, will be Samaria, built by King Omri. The south, with two tribes, will form the kingdom of Judah, with Jerusalem as capital.

Jeroboam will be elected king of Israel: on him, instead, lies the responsibility for the religious schism (1 Kings 12:26-33), with the grave consequences of the loss of unity of faith. The sin of Jeroboam was the original sin of the kingdom of Israel, continued and often made worse by the various kings who followed, nineteen in all. They ruled from 931 (Jeroboam) to 721 (Hoshea), when, with the Assyrian siege of Samaria, the Israelites were deported to Mesopotamia and Media. The kingdom never rose again (2 Kings 17:1-23).

Instead, colonies of immigrants from Syria, from Babylon… were sent to repopulate the land. To these, at later times, some Israelite survivors were joined. From this hybrid mixture arose the characteristic type of the future Samaritans, so hated by the Jews (2 Kings 17:24-41).

The Kingdom of Judah will hold out a… little longer: from 931 with Rehoboam to 587 with the last king, Zedekiah (2 Kings 25). Jerusalem will be taken, the Jews deported to Babylon. The exile will bring the definitive end of the monarchy. But God made himself continually present to assist this people: despite the divisions, the fratricidal wars, the apostasy of most of the kings, he solicitously raised up for it prophets able to warn it and constantly invite it to conversion. We have seen Samuel with Saul; Nathan with David. Elijah will be sent to King Ahab; Elisha to King Joram; Amos and Hosea to King Jeroboam; Isaiah and his disciples to the kings Ahaz and Hezekiah; Zephaniah and Nahum to King Josiah; Jeremiah will foretell to Zedekiah the seventy years of exile and will have to witness helplessly the fall of Jerusalem; Ezekiel, instead, will comfort the deportees in Babylon and prepare them for the return.

THE BOOKS OF EZRA AND NEHEMIAH

From the edict of Cyrus: 538 BC, to the building of the second Temple: 520 BC; to the restoration of the walls of Jerusalem: 443 BC; to the missions of Nehemiah and Ezra: about 400 BC.

The Birth of Judaism

Because of that promise granted by God, out of love for David, a “remnant” will return from the Babylonian exile (Ezra 1). What to human eyes may seem a… punishment becomes, for the heart of God, a correction. Painful, but it will purify the soul of this rebellious, selfish, idolatrous, superficial and arrogant people.

With the northern tribes now dispersed, the only one to return will be precisely the tribe of Judah (long since fused with that of Benjamin). The Davidic house, which the Lord reserved for himself to continue his plan of salvation, will rebuild Jerusalem (Nehemiah 2)!

A small remnant, moreover isolated in the hills of Judea, but encouraged by the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, this small state will influence, as a true hearth of rediscovered faith, the communities scattered everywhere, which could still keep the memory of the ancient covenant and attachment to the religion of the Fathers (Nehemiah 4).

After the… restoration, Yahweh reigned alone!

The one religious and civil code of the small community: the Mosaic Law. The high priest remained the true head of a people that would distinguish itself from others by a special and exclusive worship. A painful rebirth, then, and… uncompromising exclusivism!

Two centuries of calm will follow (from 400 to 198 BC), in which the small theocratic state (but with its… own currency!) will see great empires appear and decline.

With Alexander the Great the Persian era ends and the Hellenistic begins (336 BC). He will show benevolent tolerance toward the community of Jerusalem. After Alexander, Palestine passes to the rulers of Egypt: the Ptolemies (323 BC), who will maintain good relations with Jerusalem, content to collect the local tributes.

Finally it passes under the sovereignty of the Seleucids of Syria (198 BC). Only through the intrigues of the Ammonite family of the Tobiads, who wished to meddle in the internal affairs of Jerusalem, and through the influence of Hellenism on some degenerate priestly groups, does the Community suffer the persecution of the fierce Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175 – 163 BC). He wished to impose the Greek mentality and customs, dismantling the Jewish theocracy (1 Maccabees 1:1-15, 41-64).

THE MACCABEES

It is the account of the Jewish resistance to the Seleucid oppression unleashed by Antiochus.

The first book of Maccabees covers a period of 35 years: from 169 BC (Antiochus’ expedition to Egypt) to 134 BC (the year of the death of Simon Maccabeus).

The family of the Maccabees: Mattathias and his five sons will resist Antiochus’ plan to Hellenize the Jews. They will obtain, thanks to Judas Maccabeus, religious freedom (1 Maccabees 6:55ff) and the greatest independence of Judea, under Simon Maccabeus (1 Maccabees 13:41ff); though at the price of suffering and heroic witness (2 Maccabees 6 and 7).

The second book of Maccabees covers, instead, a shorter period: fifteen years, from the mission of Heliodorus (175 BC) to the victory over Nicanor (160 BC).

With John Hyrcanus (134 – 104 BC), son of Simon Maccabeus, the Hasmonean dynasty begins (the name of an ancestor of the Maccabees). His long reign saw prosperity and well-being. He was opposed by the Pharisees (earlier, by contrast, supporters of the Maccabean family), because John united priestly dignity with civil. He was succeeded by his son Aristobulus I (103 BC), then by his other son Alexander Jannaeus (102 – 76 BC), cruel and tyrannical, always in conflict with the Pharisees. On dying he advised his wife Alexandra (76 – 67 BC) to seek a policy of benevolent rapprochement with the Pharisees. Alexandra was succeeded by her son Hyrcanus II (67 BC), immediately supplanted by his younger brother Aristobulus II (67 – 63 BC). Fratricidal struggles among the last Maccabees!

Hyrcanus II, allying himself with King Aretas, tries to regain the throne. Stopped by Pompey, who occupies Jerusalem, appoints Hyrcanus II high priest and takes Aristobulus to Rome. But the Idumean Antipater, minister of Hyrcanus II, in fact governs Judea (63 – 47 BC).

Caesar appoints Hyrcanus II ethnarch, while onto the political scene steps the opportunist and bloodthirsty madman Herod, son of Antipater. By Antony, Herod will be named tetrarch! In 37 BC he will occupy Jerusalem and will be, under the name “the Great”, effective king of Judea. He will have Hyrcanus II killed in 30 BC.

We are now close to the birth of Jesus.

The history of men is exhausted in wars, divisions, the quest for domination, oppression, hatreds… Of all that they build, not one stone will be left upon another!

From the chosen people too we cannot expect anything new…

We have seen it! But because of God’s fidelity and his continual saving intervention, Israel will be purified… A “remnant”, precisely, will endure. From that remnant a “shoot” will spring! (Isaiah 11:1ff).

It is further recommended, periodically, to hold catechesis on our charism and spirituality, in particular the knowledge of the life of Mother Rose, who received that gift directly from God and faithfully lived and handed it on to the “family”.

After completing what has been indicated, the brothers are invited to a “retreat”; then, in a “celebration”, the Statute is handed over. As the biblical reading for the celebration, we recommend chapter 24 of the book of Joshua.

The journey continues with the celebrations of the Statute. At the conclusion of these celebrations, which will illuminate the spirit of the Movement, the “badge” will be given, as a sign of belonging to the Movement.

Afterwards will follow the celebrations of the fundamental themes of the charism and spirituality of the Movement: “Covenant” and “Hope”.

St. Anne, Mary and Mother Rose: three mothers who have borne children for the Church, may they help us and intercede for us, that we too may bear many other children for the Church of today!

APPENDIX

(From the Magisterial document: “CHRISTIFIDELES LAICI”)

Called to Holiness

16. The dignity of the lay faithful is revealed to us in its fullness when we consider the first and fundamental vocation that the Father addresses to each of them in Jesus Christ through the Holy Spirit: the vocation to holiness, that is, to the perfection of charity. The saint is the most splendid witness of the dignity conferred on the disciple of Christ.

The Second Vatican Council has spoken in most luminous words on the universal call to holiness. One can say that this was precisely the primary charge entrusted to all the sons and daughters of the Church by a Council intended for the evangelical renewal of Christian life.
