This charge is not a simple moral exhortation, but an irrepressible requirement of the mystery of the Church: she is the chosen vineyard, through which the branches live and grow with the very holy and sanctifying sap of Christ; she is the mystical body, whose members share in the same life of holiness as the Head, who is Christ; she is the Bride beloved of the Lord Jesus, who gave himself up to sanctify her (cf. Eph 5:25ff). The Spirit who sanctified the human nature of Jesus in the virginal womb of Mary (cf. Lk 1:35) is the same Spirit who dwells and works in the Church to communicate to her the holiness of the Son of God made man.

It is more urgent than ever that today all Christians take up again the path of evangelical renewal, welcoming with generosity the apostolic invitation to “be holy in all your conduct” (1 Pet 1:15). The extraordinary Synod of 1985, twenty years after the close of the Council, fittingly insisted on this urgency: “Since the Church in Christ is a mystery, she must be considered the sign and instrument of holiness (…). The saints have always been the source and origin of renewal in the most difficult circumstances throughout the Church’s history. Today we have the greatest need of saints, whom we must implore from God with assiduity.”

All in the Church, precisely because they are her members, receive and therefore share in the common vocation to holiness. In full right, without any difference from the other members of the Church, the lay faithful are called to it: “All the faithful of whatever state or rank are called to the fullness of Christian life and to the perfection of charity”; “All the faithful are invited and bound to strive for holiness and the perfection of their own state.”

The call to holiness is rooted in Baptism and is set before us again by the other sacraments, principally by the Eucharist: clothed in Jesus Christ and refreshed by his Spirit, Christians are “holy” and are therefore enabled and committed to manifest the holiness of their being in the holiness of all their conduct. The apostle Paul never tires of admonishing all Christians to live “as is fitting among saints” (Eph 5:3).

Life according to the Spirit, whose fruit is sanctification (cf. Rom 6:22; Gal 5:22), arouses and requires of every baptised person and of each the following and imitation of Jesus Christ, in the acceptance of his beatitudes, in listening to and meditating on the word of God, in conscious and active participation in the liturgical and sacramental life of the Church, in individual, family and community prayer, in hunger and thirst for justice, in the practice of the commandment of love in all circumstances of life and in service to the brethren, especially if they are little, poor and suffering.

Sanctifying Oneself in the World

17. The vocation of the lay faithful to holiness implies that life according to the Spirit be expressed in a particular way in their involvement in temporal realities and in their participation in earthly activities. Once again it is the apostle who admonishes us: “Whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him” (Col 3:17). Applying the apostle’s words to the lay faithful, the Council categorically states: “Neither the care of the family nor other secular duties should be foreign to the spiritual orientation of life.” For their part, the Synod Fathers said: “The unity of life of the lay faithful is of the greatest importance: indeed, they must be sanctified in ordinary professional and social life. Therefore, in order that they may respond to their vocation, the lay faithful must view the activities of daily life as an occasion of union with God and of fulfilling his will, as well as of service to other people, leading them to communion with God in Christ.”

The vocation to holiness must be perceived and lived by the lay faithful, before it is a demanding and unrenounceable obligation, as a luminous sign of the Father’s infinite love who has regenerated them to his life of holiness. Such a vocation, then, must be called an essential and inseparable component of the new baptismal life, and therefore a constitutive element of their dignity. At the same time the vocation to holiness is intimately connected with the mission and responsibility entrusted to the lay faithful in the Church and in the world. Indeed, holiness lived, which derives from participation in the Church’s life of holiness, already represents the first and fundamental contribution to the building up of the Church herself as the “Communion of Saints.” Before eyes enlightened by faith a wonderful scene opens: that of countless lay faithful, men and women, who precisely in the life and activities of each day, often unnoticed or even misunderstood, unknown to the great of the earth but looked upon with love by the Father, are the tireless workers who labour in the Lord’s vineyard, the humble and great builders – certainly by the power of God’s grace – of the growth of the kingdom of God in history.

Holiness, moreover, must be called a fundamental presupposition and a wholly irreplaceable condition for the fulfilment of the mission of salvation within the Church. It is the holiness of the Church that is the secret source and the infallible measure of her apostolic zeal and missionary drive. Only to the extent that the Church, Bride of Christ, lets herself be loved by him and loves him in return, does she become a fruitful Mother in the Spirit.

Let us take up the biblical image again: the blossoming and spreading of the branches depend on their being grafted onto the vine. “As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it remains on the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me. I am the vine, you are the branches. Whoever remains in me and I in him will bear much fruit, because without me you can do nothing” (Jn 15:4-5).

It is natural here to recall the solemn proclamation of lay faithful, men and women, as blessed and saints, which took place during the month of the Synod. The whole people of God, and the lay faithful in particular, can now find new models of holiness and new witnesses of heroic virtues lived in the common and ordinary conditions of human existence. As the Synod Fathers said: “The local Churches and above all the so-called younger Churches must attentively recognize among their members those men and women who have offered in such conditions (the daily conditions of the world and the married state) the witness of holiness and who can be an example to others, so that, should the case arise, they may propose them for beatification and canonization.”

At the end of these reflections, meant to define the ecclesial condition of the lay faithful, there comes to mind the celebrated admonition of St. Leo the Great: “Agnosce, o Christiane, dignitatem tuam” (“Recognize, O Christian, your dignity”). And the same admonition of St. Maximus, Bishop of Turin, addressed to those who had received the anointing of holy Baptism: “Consider the honor that is done to you in this mystery!” All the baptised are invited to listen again to the words of St. Augustine: “Let us rejoice and give thanks: we have become not only Christians, but Christ (…). Marvel and rejoice: we have become Christ!”

Christian dignity, the source of equality for all members of the Church, guarantees and promotes the spirit of communion and fraternity and, at the same time, becomes the secret and the strength of the apostolic and missionary dynamism of the lay faithful. It is a demanding dignity, the dignity of the workers called by the Lord to labour in his vineyard: “Upon all the laity – we read in the Council – rests the glorious burden of working so that the divine plan of salvation may reach more and more all people of all times and all places.”
